texts.preamble: Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023
texts.facts: Petitioner - Prithi Pal Singh has filed the present petition, under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as 'CrPC') read with Article 227 of the Constitution of India, for setting aside the order, dated 29th June, 2019, passed by the Court of learned Sessions Judge, Kangra at Dharamshala. dismissed the revision petition, filed by the petitioner, against the summoning order, dated 28 th November, 2000, passed by the Court of learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Kangra at Dharamshala (hereinafter referred to as 'the trial of Court') in Complaint Case No. 103-I/2002. 3. Thert parties to the present petition, are hereinafter, referred to, in the same manner, in which, they were referred to, by the learned trial Court. 4. Brief facts, leading to the filing of the present petition, before this Court, as per the record, may be summed up, as under: 4.1. Drugs Inspector-Navneet Marwaha has filed a complaint, under Section 18 (c) read with Section 27 (b) (ii) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act'), against accused-Prithi Pal Singh, who has been impleaded in the complaint, as Managing Director of M/s Raman Pharmaceuticals Private Limited, 233, Tea Estate Road, Dharamshala, H.P. 4.2. The said complaint has been filed, on the ground, that on 14th February, 1989, one purchase order . was placed by the then Chief Medical officer, Kangra at Dharamshala, namely Dr. B.S. Vakil to M/s Raman Pharmaceuticals for supplying Phenitone - 60 (Phenobarbitone Tablets) (hereinafter referred to as the of 'drug in question'), vide order No. ACTT/89-660, dated 14 th February, 1989. rt 4.3. In pursuance of the same, 45,000/- tablets of Phenitone-60 were supplied by the said firm, vide invoice No. 603, dated 24th March, 1989. Thereafter, the accused received the payment of 4,608/- from the office of Chief Medical Officer, Kangra at Dharamshala, vide receipt No. 003451, dated 20th February, 2020. 4.4 . It is the further case of the complainant that in the month of March, 1997, it was transpired that the accused person was not having a valid drug licence to manufacture the tablets, which were supplied to the Chief Medical Officer, Dharamshala, as, the same falls under Schedule X of the Act. When, this fact came to the notice, then, the Drugs Controller, Himachal Pradesh, order to investigate the matter and thereafter, the complaint has been filed. . 4.5. As per the complainant, during investigation, office of the Chief Medical Officer, Kangra at Dharamshala, was requested to supply the requisite documents, upon which, on 8th April, 1999, it has been informed that the of requisite record has already been seized by the Vigilance Department, Dharamshala, in connection with some other rt case. Thereafter, a request was made to the office of Deputy Superintendent of Police, Anti Corruption Zone, Dharamshala, to provide the requisite Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170138737/ 2 record. On this communication, it has been informed that the case file is pending disposal before the Court of learned Special Judge, Dharamshala, in Case FIR No. 2/91, dated 1 st July, 1991, under Section 22 of the Himachal Pradesh Prevention of Specific Corrupt Practices Act, with Police Station, Dharamshala. 4.6. In nut shell, it is the case of the complainant that without a valid drug licence, the accused has supplied the drugs, in contravention of Section 18 (c) of the Act. 5. On the basis of the said complaint, the complainant appeared in the witness box and produced the . documents, Ex. CW-1/A to Ex. CW-1/N. 6. After perusing the said complaint, evidence of CW-1 (complainant) and the documents produced by him, the learned trial Court found a prima facie case for the of commission of offences, punishable under Section 18 (c) read with Section 27 (b) (ii) of the Act. rt As such, the accused was ordered to be summoned for 17 th January, 2001. 7. The said order had been assailed by the accused, by moving Criminal Revision, bearing Case No. 16-D/X/2015, titled as Prithi Pal Singh versus State of Himachal Pradesh, before the Court of learned Sessions Judge, Kangra at Dharamshala , however, the said Revision Petition has been dismissed, vide order, dated 29 th June, 2019. 8. Feeling aggrieved from the said order, the present petition has been filed, before this Court, on the ground that it has mainly been mentioned in the complaint that the Drugs Inspector came to know, in the month of March, 1997, that the accused company did not possess a valid drug licence, for manufacturing the drugs, which . have been supplied. 9. As a matter of fact, according to the accused, the drugs were supplied in the year 1989, however, on 6 th March, 1990, one FIR No. 2/1991, under Section 22 of the of Himachal Pradesh Prevention of Specific Corrupt Practices Act, was registered against the then Chief Medical Officer, rt Kangra at Dharamshala, Dr. B.S. Vakil, as well as, the accused (petitioner herein). The said FIR has been lodged by one Shakti Chand, who was working as Pharmacist in the office of Chief Medical Officer, Dharamshala. 10. As per the accused, in the said FIR, allegations were levelled that M/s Raman Pharmaceuticals was not having a manufacturing licence to manufacture the drug in question and despite this fact, the then Chief Medical Officer, Kangra at Dharamshala, had issued the supply order to the said Company. After the investigation, the police had submitted the cancellation report, on the ground, that the Company has made the supply to the Chief Medical Officer, Kangra at Dharamshala, before 1 st May, 1991 and it had a valid licence till 27 th December, 1991, whereafter, the Company did not Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170138737/ 3 renew the said . licence. The said cancellation report was accepted by the Special Judge, Kangra at Dharamshala, vide order, dated 15th February, 2002. 11. On the basis of the above facts, the accused of intends to establish the fact that at the relevant time, the Company had a valid manufacturing licence. According to rt the accused, the relevant date was when the supply was made. 12. From these submissions, the accused intend to establish that the office of the Chief Medical Officer, Kangra at Dharamshala was aware about the said controversy and as such, the assertion, as made in para-5 of the complaint, is wrong. 13. . 15. On the basis of the above facts, a prayer has been made to allow the petition, by quashing the summoning order, as well as, the complaint. As stated above, the accused has assailed the summoning order, passed by the learned trial Court, on of 28th November, 2000, before the learned Sessions Judge, Kangra at Dharamshala, by way of Revision Petition. rt When, the said Revision Petition has been dismissed, he has filed the present petition, before this Court, under Section 482 CrPC. 21.
texts.arguments: The other ground of attack is that the mandatory provisions of Section 34 of the Act have not been complied with, as, the accused is not the incharge of the affairs of the Company. 16. The prayer, so made, in the petition, has been of opposed by Mr. Mohinder Zharaick, learned Additional Advocate General, appearing for the respondent-State, on rt the ground that whatsoever pleaded by the accused, before this Court, is nothing, but, his defence, which will be considered by the learned trial Court, during the trial of the case. 17. It has also been argued by the learned Additional Advocate General that the accused has not appeared before the learned trial Court and, as such, he has been declared as proclaimed offender, by the learned trial Court, vide order, dated 29 th December, 2004 and the accused, in stead of moving the appropriate application, before the learned trial Court, had firstly filed the revision before the learned Sessions Judge and after the dismissal of the same, the present petition has been filed. 18. Hence, a prayer has been made to dismiss the petition. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in a case, titled as, State of Haryana versus Bhajanlal, reported in 1992 Supp(1) SCC 335, has laid down the following guidelines, for the exercise of the powers, under Section 482 of Cr PC: "(1) where the allegations made in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused; (2) where the allegations in the First Information Report and other materials, if any, accompanying the F.I.R. do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code; (3) where the uncontroverted allegations made . in the FIR or 'complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused; (4) where the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation of is permitted by a police officer without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code; rt (5) where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused; (6) where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party; (7) where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge." 22. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in another case, titled as, Madhavrao Jiwajirao Scindia Vs. Sambhajirao Chadrojirao Angre, reported in (1988) 1 SCC 692, has also summarized the law, with Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170138737/ 5 regard to quashing of criminal proceedings, under Section 482 CrPC. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in a case, titled as Harshendra Kumar D versus Rebatilata Koley and others, reported in (2011) 3 Supreme Court Cases 351, has held that the public document, or the document, . which are beyond suspicion or doubt, can be looked into, by the High Court, in exercise of its jurisdiction, under Section 482 CrPC. Relevant paras 25 and 26 of the judgment, are reproduced as under: of "25. In such a matter, for promotion of justice or to prevent injustice or abuse of process, the High Court may look Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170138737/ 6 into the materials which have significant bearing on the matter at prima facie stage. 26. Criminal prosecution is a serious matter; it affects the liberty of a person. No greater damage can be done to the reputation of a person than dragging him in a criminal case. 25. This view has again been reiterated by a three of Judges Bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case, titled as Mohd. Akram Siddiqui versus State of Bihar and rt another, reported in (2019) 13 Supreme Court Cases 350. Relevant para-5 of the judgment, is reproduced, as under: "5. However an exception has been carved out by this Court in Yin Cheng Hsiung v. Essem Chemical Industries, (2011) 15 SCC 207; State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335; and Harshendra Kumar D. v. Rebatilata Koley, (2011) 3 SCC 351, to the effect that in an appropriate case where the document relied upon is a public document or where veracity thereof is not disputed by the complainant, the same can be considered." (self emphasis supplied) 26. 28 . It would be apt to record herein that as the of amendment has been carried out, in this Section, with effect from 10th August, 2009. (b) any drug - (i) ... ... ... (ii) without a valid licence as required under clause (c) of Section 18, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to three years and with fine which shall not be less than five thousand rupees." 29. Section 468 CrPC creates a bar to taking of cognizance, after lapse of the period of limitation. It would be profitable to reproduce Section 468 CrPC, as under: rt "468. Bar to taking cognizance after lapse of the period of limitation. - (1) Except as otherwise provided elsewhere in this Code, no Court shall take cognizance of an offence of the category specified in sub- section (2), after the expiry of the period of limitation. (2) The period of limitation shall be- (a) six months, if the offence is punishable with fine only; (b) one year, if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year; (c) three years, if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for term exceeding one year but not exceeding three years. (3) For the purposes of this section, the period of limitation in relation to offences which may be tried together, shall be determined with reference to the offence which is punishable with the more severe punishment or, as the case may be, the most severe punishment." 31. It would also be apt to reproduce Section 469 CrPC, as under: Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170138737/ 8 . "469. Commencement of the period of limitation. - (1) The period of limitation, in relation to an offence, shall commence, - (a) on the date of the offence; or (b) where the commission of the offence was not known to the person aggrieved by the offence or to any police officer, the first day of on which such offence comes to the knowledge of such person or to any police officer, whichever is earlier; or (c)rt where it is not known by whom the offence was committed, the first day on which the identity of the offender is known to the person aggrieved by the offence or to the police officer making investigation into the offence, whichever is earlier. (2) In computing the said period, the day from which such period is to be computed shall be excluded." Section 34 of the Act is reproduced as under: "34. Offences by companies.-- (1) Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly: Provided that nothing contained in this sub- section shall render any such person liable to any punishment provided in this Act if he proves that . the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub- section (1), where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the of consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall rt also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. Explanation.--For the purposes of this section-- (a) "company" means a body corporate, and includes a firm or other association of individuals; and (b) "director" in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm." 46. The relevance and importance of this Section has elaborately been discussed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as State of NCT of Delhi through Prosecuting Officer, Insecticides, Government of NCT, Delhi versus Rajiv Khurana, reported in (2011) 1 Supreme Court Cases (Cri) 195. Relevant paras-14 and 20 of the judgment, are reproduced, as under: "14. The respondent placed reliance on S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd., (2005) 8 SCC 89, wherein this Court has held as under. (SCC p. 103, para 19) "19. Similar view has been taken by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in another case, titled as Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited versus Food Inspector and another, reported in (2011) 1 Supreme Court Cases 176. In this case, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has discussed the provisions of Section 17 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which are almost pari materia to the provisions of Section 34 of the Prithi Pal Singh vs Of on 11 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170138737/ 13 Act. 49. On this . score, the accused is entitled for the relief, as claimed.
